guide.title: Pinciano, Rome: Villa Borghese, the Galleria Borghese and the academies of Valle Giulia
guide.intro: Pinciano is the third quartiere of Rome, Q. III in Roma Capitale's toponymic series, code 203, and it sits in Municipio Roma II. Much of what brings a visitor here stands inside Villa Borghese, eighty hectares of park north of the Aurelian Walls: the Galleria Borghese in the family's own casino, the national gallery of modern art and the Etruscan museum of Villa Giulia along its edge, a zoo, a children's museum, four small theatres and cinemas, and eighteenth-century temples, gates and fountains scattered down the avenues. Outside the park are the foreign academies of Valle Giulia, four parish churches, two catacombs cut under residential streets, a mausoleum and a late-antique hypogeum, and a belt of villini built between 1900 and 1930 with a named architect on almost every one. The Pincio is not part of this quartiere: the walls are the line, and everything south of them is the rione Campo Marzio.

sections.heading: The edges of the quartiere
sections.body:
Pinciano's edges are streets, and it.wikipedia's article on the quartiere names each of them with the neighbour on the far side. Viale Maresciallo Pilsudski, viale dei Parioli and viale Liegi as far as via Salaria divide it from Q. II Parioli. Via Salaria, from viale Regina Margherita to piazza Fiume, divides it from Q. IV Salario. The walls, running behind Corso d'Italia from piazza Fiume to piazzale Brasile at Porta Pinciana, divide it from the rione Ludovisi; the walls again, behind viale del Muro Torto from Porta Pinciana to piazzale Flaminio at Porta del Popolo, divide it from the rione Campo Marzio. Via Flaminia, from piazzale Flaminio to viale Maresciallo Pilsudski, divides it from Q. I Flaminio.

The Aurelian Walls are the line. Villa Borghese's own account says the park lies largely in the quartiere Pinciano and in small part in the rione Campo Marzio, the two divided by the walls. On the Campo Marzio side stand the Pincio terrace and promenade, Piazzale Napoleone I, the Pincio obelisk, the busts and the avenue statues, the water clock, the monuments to the Cairoli brothers and to Enrico Toti, the Fontana della Vasca, the convent of Santa Rita, the Casina Valadier, the Muro Torto, Villa Medici, Porta del Popolo and Piazza del Popolo.

Two more names catch people out, in opposite directions. Piazzale Flaminio is described by its own source as divided between the quartieri Pinciano and Flaminio; addresses on it are usable, and Villa Borghese's neoclassical propylaea stand there. The church of Sant'Andrea del Vignola, on the same stretch of via Flaminia as Explora, places itself in the quartiere Flaminio in its own opening line. Going the other way, two names that sound like Parioli are in fact Pinciano's: Villa Balestra, which occupies a spur of the Parioli hills and is reached from via Bartolomeo Ammannati, and the church of Santa Maria della Pace ai Parioli on viale Bruno Buozzi, both of which say so in their own articles.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
The quartiere's transport corner is piazzale Flaminio, where metro line A has its Flaminio station and the Roma-Viterbo railway has its terminus. Both are the usual way in to the southern end of Villa Borghese, and the propylaea are the gate you walk through.

Two operators publish their own directions, and those are the ones to follow. La Galleria Nazionale gives metro line A to Flaminio, about 600 metres away; trams 3 and 19 along viale delle Belle Arti; buses 61, 89, 160, 490, 495 and M at piazzale del Fiocco; and the Roma-Viterbo line to Flaminio station. The Bioparco gives tram 19 to the stop named Bioparco; buses 3, 52, 53, 217, 360 and 926, and bus 910, which stops at the entrance only on Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays; and metro line A to Flaminio or Spagna.

The Sovrintendenza Capitolina lists nine ways into Villa Borghese: via Aldrovandi, two entrances on via Raimondi, two on via Pinciana, piazzale San Paolo del Brasile, piazzale Flaminio, piazzale Cervantes and piazzale Pablo Picasso on via di Valle Giulia. For everything else, steer by the address. The Galleria Borghese is at Piazzale Scipione Borghese 5, 00197. La Galleria Nazionale is at Viale delle Belle Arti 131, 00197. The Etruscan museum is at Piazzale di Villa Giulia 9, 00196, with Villa Poniatowski round the corner at Via di Villa Giulia 34. The Bioparco's public entrance is at Piazzale del Giardino Zoologico 1, its administrative address Viale del Giardino Zoologico 20, 00197, and the Museo Civico di Zoologia, which physically adjoins it, is at Via Ulisse Aldrovandi 18, 00197. The Museo Pietro Canonica is at Viale Pietro Canonica 2, 00197, on Piazza di Siena. Explora is at Via Flaminia 80/86, 00196. The British School is at Via Antonio Gramsci 61, 00197, and the Accademia di Danimarca at Via Omero 18, 00197.

sections.heading: Tickets and opening hours
sections.body:
Villa Borghese is open daily from dawn to dusk. Roma Capitale's tourism service states that the opening and closing of the gates is contracted to Risorse per Roma until 31 December 2027, with the gates worked between 06.30 and 08.30 and again between 17.00 and 19.00 from November to February, between 19.00 and 21.00 in March, April, September and October, and between 20.00 and 22.00 from May to August.

The anchor museum is the awkward one. The Galleria Borghese's own site gives its address, its telephone number and a booking line, and no source states its opening hours, so none are given here. Everything else in the park does publish. La Galleria Nazionale opens Tuesday to Sunday, 08.30 to 19.30, last admission forty-five minutes before closing, shut on Mondays, 1 January and 25 December, at 10.00 euro full and 5.00 euro reduced. The Museo Nazionale Etrusco at Villa Giulia opens Tuesday to Sunday 08.30 to 19.30, with the rooms closing at 19.00 and last entry at 18.30, at 13.00 euro full and 2.00 euro reduced. The Museo Pietro Canonica and the Museo Carlo Bilotti share the civic-museum tariff, 7.50 euro full and 6.00 euro reduced, or 11.00 and 7.50 when an exhibition is running, with the annual MIC card at 5.00 euro; both close on Mondays, 1 May and 25 December, and both run shorter winter hours than summer ones, so check the season. The Bioparco is open every day of the year except 25 December, 09.30 to 17.00 from 1 January to 28 March, 09.30 to 18.00 from 29 March to 24 October and 09.30 to 17.00 from 25 October to 31 December, with a 19.00 closing on Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays between 29 March and 4 October; the ticket desks and last admission are an hour before closing, and the standard ticket is 19.00 euro.

Three places are for children and each has its own timetable. Explora, the children's museum on via Flaminia, admits in four sessions of an hour and three quarters, at 10.00, 12.00, 15.00 and 17.00, Tuesday to Sunday, closed Mondays. The Casina di Raffaello, the park's playroom for ages three to fourteen, opens Tuesday to Friday 10.00 to 18.00 and Saturdays, Sundays and holidays 10.00 to 19.00 in its spring and autumn season, and closes on Mondays, 1 January, Easter Monday, 1 May, 25 December and from 9 to 23 August. The Cinema dei Piccoli, sixty-three seats on viale della Pineta, publishes a telephone number, +39 06 8553485, and no standard ticket price.

The ancient sites are the other way round: two of them are shut. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives the Mausoleo di Lucilio Peto on via Salaria as temporarily closed, and the Ipogeo di via Livenza as closed to the public for works under the PNRR. When the hypogeum reopens, its published terms are accompanied groups only, a maximum of ten people per visit, booking on 060608 between 09.00 and 19.00, and 4.00 euro full or 3.00 euro reduced, with the guided tour not included. The catacombs of San Panfilo and Sant'Ermete publish nothing at all about access.

faq.question: When is the Galleria Borghese open?
faq.answer: No source states its opening hours, so none are given here. What the museum's own site does give is the address, Piazzale Scipione Borghese 5, 00197 Roma, a telephone number, +39 06 8413979, and a separate booking line, +39 06 32810. Entry is by timed slot, and the site's own standing notice warns about unauthorised resellers. The collection was formed by Cardinal Scipione Borghese and includes Bernini's David and Apollo e Dafne and Canova's Paolina Borghese; the Italian state acquired it in 1902, and the museum closed in 1983 and reopened in June 1997.

faq.question: Is the Pincio part of Villa Borghese, and is it in Pinciano?
faq.answer: The Pincio adjoins the park and is walked as part of it, but it is not in this quartiere. Villa Borghese's own account states that the park lies largely in the quartiere Pinciano and in small part in the rione Campo Marzio, and that the two parts are divided by the Aurelian Walls. The Pincio terrace and promenade, Piazzale Napoleone I, the Pincio obelisk, the water clock, the Casina Valadier, the Muro Torto, Villa Medici and Piazza del Popolo are all south of the walls, in the rione Campo Marzio.

faq.question: What is there for children?
faq.answer: Four things, all with published hours or contact details. The Bioparco, the zoological garden inside the park, is open every day of the year except 25 December and holds about 1,200 animals of about 150 species. Explora, on via Flaminia, admits in four timed sessions a day, Tuesday to Sunday. The Casina di Raffaello is Villa Borghese's playroom for ages three to fourteen, with a small area for under-threes. The Cinema dei Piccoli on viale della Pineta has sixty-three seats and a screen five metres by two and a half.

faq.question: Can you go inside the catacombs and the mausoleum?
faq.answer: Not at present, and in two cases nobody says. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina states that the Mausoleo di Lucilio Peto on via Salaria is temporarily closed and that the Ipogeo di via Livenza is closed for works under the PNRR; the hypogeum's published terms for when it reopens are accompanied groups of no more than ten, booked on 060608, at 4.00 euro full and 3.00 euro reduced. The catacombs of San Panfilo, under via Paisiello and via Spontini, and of Sant'Ermete, on via Bertoloni, are in the care of the Pontificia Commissione di Archeologia Sacra, and no source states whether or how they can be visited, so nothing is given here.

faq.question: There are embassies and academies everywhere. Which can be visited?
faq.answer: Valle Giulia, the small valley between Villa Borghese and the Parioli hill, has held foreign research institutes since the 1911 national exposition: the British School at Rome in Edwin Lutyens's building on via Antonio Gramsci, the Accademia di Danimarca on via Omero, the Forum Austriaco di Cultura on viale Bruno Buozzi, the Istituto Giapponese di Cultura on via Antonio Gramsci, and the Dutch, Belgian, Swedish and Romanian institutes. They are residential research bodies that publish events, exhibitions and libraries rather than general opening hours. Two nearby buildings are working diplomatic missions and are not open at all: Villa Giorgina on via Po, the Apostolic Nunciature to Italy, and Palazzo Borromeo on viale delle Belle Arti, which has housed Italy's embassy to the Holy See since 1929. Both stand on Italian soil, and neither is open to visitors.

places.name: Villa Borghese
places.address: Piazzale San Paolo del Brasile, 00197 Roma RM
places.summary: Eighty hectares of historic park. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records it as being in Municipio II, quartiere Pinciano, gives its extent as eighty hectares and lists nine entrances: via Aldrovandi, two on via Raimondi, two on via Pinciana, piazzale San Paolo del Brasile, piazzale Flaminio, piazzale Cervantes and piazzale Pablo Picasso on via di Valle Giulia. Villa Borghese is open daily from dawn to dusk. Roma Capitale's tourism service states that the opening and closing of the gates is contracted to Risorse per Roma until 31 December 2027, with the gates worked between 06.30 and 08.30 and again between 17.00 and 19.00 from November to February, between 19.00 and 21.00 in March, April, September and October, and between 20.00 and 22.00 from May to August. Metro line A has its Flaminio station and the Roma-Viterbo railway its terminus at piazzale Flaminio, at the park's western corner.
places.history: The core was already Borghese property in 1580. Cardinal Scipione Borghese, nephew of Paul V, began building in 1606, giving the works to Flaminio Ponzio and, after Ponzio's death, to the Fleming Giovanni Vasanzio; the villa was completed in 1633. In 1766 Prince Marcantonio IV Borghese commissioned Antonio Asprucci and his son Mario to remodel the casino, the Casino dei giuochi d'acqua and above all the park, where they laid out the Giardino del Lago. In the early nineteenth century Camillo Borghese bought land toward porta del Popolo and porta Pinciana and had Luigi Canina knit it into the whole. The Italian state bought the complex in 1901 and ceded it to the comune of Rome in 1903, for three million lire of the day, so that it would be permanently open to the public; its official name became Villa comunale Umberto I gia Borghese, and Romans went on calling it Villa Borghese. Its own account says the park lies largely in the quartiere Pinciano and in small part in the rione Campo Marzio, divided by the Aurelian Walls. Roma Capitale calls it, in quotation marks of its own, the Parco dei Musei. Two smaller buildings are named on the villa's own lists without a date or an author: the Casina dell'Orologio and the Prospettiva del Teatro on viale Fiorello La Guardia, whose facade is brightly decorated. Roma Capitale's tourism service also lists a puppet theatre among the park's services.

places.name: Galleria Borghese
places.summary: The state museum inside the Villa Borghese Pinciana, the casino Scipione Borghese built for himself, holding the collection he began. Its own site gives the address as Piazzale Scipione Borghese 5, 00197 Roma, the telephone number +39 06 8413979, a booking line on +39 06 32810 and the address ga-bor.info@cultura.gov.it. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here. It recorded 590,891 visitors in 2023. Among the works are Bernini's David and Apollo e Dafne and Canova's Paolina Borghese come Venere Vittoriosa in the Sala della Paolina; the collection also holds Bronzino, Caravaggio, Raffaello, Perugino, Lorenzo Lotto, Antonello da Messina, Cranach, Annibale Carracci, Rubens, Bellini and Tiziano.
places.history: The house is the one Flaminio Ponzio began in 1606 from Scipione Borghese's sketches and Giovanni Vasanzio finished after Ponzio's death, complete in 1633; its facade was originally set with 144 bas-reliefs and seventy busts, Lodovico Cigoli frescoed a Story of Psyche inside, and the windows and the sequence of rooms were laid out to show the sculpture and painting well. The Borghese picture gallery, until then in via Ripetta, moved up to the piano nobile in 1891. In 1902 the Italian state acquired the Fidecommisso Borghese collections and the villa, and the museum opened under its first director Giovanni Piancastelli, succeeded in 1906 by Giulio Cantalamessa. It closed in 1983 and reopened in June 1997 after a fourteen-year restoration, has held special autonomy among Italy's state museums since 2014, and has been directed by Francesca Cappelletti since November 2020.

places.name: La Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea
places.address: Viale delle Belle Arti 131, 00197 Roma RM
places.summary: The national gallery of modern and contemporary art, on the Valle Giulia side of the park. Its own site gives Viale delle Belle Arti 131, 00197 Roma, telephone +39 06 322981, and opening Tuesday to Sunday from 08.30 to 19.30, with last admission forty-five minutes before closing and closure on Mondays, 1 January and 25 December. Tickets are 10.00 euro full and 5.00 euro reduced, the reduction covering EU citizens aged 18 to 25 and teachers in EU state schools; entry is free for under-18s, journalists with a valid card, tourist guides, ICOM members and Ministry staff, and on the first Sunday of the month, and reduced for holders of a MAXXI or Museo delle Civilta ticket. An audio guide in Italian and English is 5.00 euro. The museum's own visitor rules permit photography without flash and amateur video. Its accessibility statement lists lifts, lift platforms and two wheelchairs, including for independent use. It gives its transport as metro line A to Flaminio, about 600 metres; trams 3 and 19 on viale delle Belle Arti; buses 61, 89, 160, 490, 495 and M at piazzale del Fiocco; and the Roma-Viterbo line to Flaminio.
places.history: The building was put up for the 1911 Esposizione nazionale to a design by Cesare Bazzani, in the Valle Giulia laid out for that exhibition.

places.name: Museo Nazionale Etrusco di Villa Giulia (ETRU)
places.address: Piazzale di Villa Giulia 9, 00196 Roma RM
places.summary: The state museum of Etruscan and Faliscan antiquities from Lazio, southern Etruria and Umbria, in Julius III's suburban villa. Its own site gives Piazzale di Villa Giulia 9, opening Tuesday to Sunday 08.30 to 19.30 with the rooms closing at 19.00 and last entry at 18.30, and tickets at 13.00 euro full and 2.00 euro reduced, with free entry on the first Sunday of the month. The named holdings include the Sarcofago degli Sposi, a terracotta funerary monument showing a near life-size couple reclining at a banquet; the Lamine di Pyrgi; the Apollo di Veio; the remains and reconstruction of the Etruscan temple of Alatri; the Pyrgi high relief with the Seven against Thebes; the Barberini, Castellani and Pesciotti collections; the Cista Ficoroni; and the Olpe Chigi. The villa and the museum share an address, an operator and a door, and are one place.
places.history: The villa was built as Julius III's suburban residence between 1551 and 1553 to designs by Vignola, Giorgio Vasari and Bartolomeo Ammannati. The museum was founded in 1889 by Felice Barnabei. It has held special autonomy since 2016, recorded 80,266 visitors in 2023, and has been directed by Luana Toniolo since 16 May 2024. In 2012 it opened rooms in the neighbouring Villa Poniatowski. It is the venue of the Premio Strega final.

places.name: Villa Poniatowski
places.address: Via di Villa Giulia 34, 00196 Roma RM
places.summary: The second seat of the Museo Nazionale Etrusco, holding Etrusco-Italic material from Latium vetus and Umbria, including parts of the grave goods of the Barberini and Bernardini tombs of Palestrina and remains of the temple of Mater Matuta at Satricum. No separate opening times are published for it.
places.history: Cardinal Pierdonato Cesi bought the land around 1570 and Montaigne described the place in 1581; a Venturini engraving of 1683 shows it as Borromeo property. It passed from the Cesi to the Sinibaldi in 1702, to the Candelori in 1798, and then to Prince Stanislaw Poniatowski, who had Giuseppe Valadier rebuild the sixteenth-century casino and the terraced Italian garden. It was badly damaged in the fighting of 1849 between Garibaldini and French troops, and the Riganti family put a tannery in the garden after 1870. The Italian state bought it in 1988, recovery works were carried out in 1998 for the 2000 Jubilee, and it was inaugurated as a museum seat in 2012.

places.name: Bioparco di Roma
places.address: Viale del Giardino Zoologico 20, 00197 Roma RM
places.summary: The zoological garden of Rome, inside Villa Borghese. Its own site gives the public entrance as Piazzale del Giardino Zoologico 1 and the administrative address as Viale del Giardino Zoologico 20, 00197 Roma. It holds about 1,200 animals of about 150 species of mammals, reptiles and birds, over about 155,480 square metres, and recorded 552,468 visitors in 2022. For 2026 it publishes 09.30 to 17.00 from 1 January to 28 March, 09.30 to 18.00 from 29 March to 24 October and 09.30 to 17.00 from 25 October to 31 December, with a 19.00 closing on Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays between 29 March and 4 October; ticket desks and last admission are an hour before closing, and the park is open every day of the year except 25 December. Tickets are 19.00 euro full and 14.00 euro reduced for children over one metre tall up to ten years old, for over-65s and for groups of fifteen or more visiting freely, and 11.00 euro for disabled visitors with recognised invalidity below 100 per cent; entry is free for children under one metre and for visitors with 100 per cent recognised invalidity plus a companion. A last-minute ticket at 9.00 euro can be bought two hours before closing, and 2026 six-month open passes are 20.00 and 16.00 euro. Its own transport directions give tram 19 to the Bioparco stop, buses 3, 52, 53, 217, 360 and 926, bus 910 stopping at the entrance only at weekends and on holidays, and metro line A to Flaminio or Spagna.
places.history: Rome's council resolved to create a zoological garden inside Villa Umberto I in 1907; the operating company was formed in 1909, chaired first by Baron Giorgio Sonnino and then by Prince Francesco Chigi, on ground between via delle Tre Madonne and the land of Villa Taverna; the garden opened in 1911. The company engaged Carl Hagenbeck, whose Hamburg Tierpark had introduced barless enclosures modelled on habitat, and whose scheme for about twelve hectares with a large restaurant was presented at the Hotel Excelsior on 12 November 1908; the contract of 8 May 1909 gave forty-five years' use, after which the buildings passed to the comune. Moritz Lehmann did the decoration and Ernest Eggenschwiler the rockwork, Giuseppe Roda the planting, and Giulio Barluzzi with Armando Brasini the monumental entrance. It was renamed Bioparco at the end of the twentieth century and is run by the Fondazione Bioparco di Roma, controlled by Roma Capitale. The Portale dei vasi was moved from Porta Pinciana to the zoo entrance in 1914.

places.name: Museo Civico di Zoologia
places.summary: The civic zoological museum, one of the scientific museums of the Sistema Musei di Roma Capitale, at Via Ulisse Aldrovandi 18. It physically adjoins the Bioparco. Its named holdings include the Collezione Monterosato of shells and the ornithological Collezione Arrigoni degli Oddi, the Sala degli scheletri, the standing exhibition Vivere al limite and the ZooLab. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states an institutional history of the museum.

places.name: Museo Pietro Canonica a Villa Borghese
places.summary: The sculptor Pietro Canonica's museum, in the building called the Fortezzuola, on Piazza di Siena. Its own site gives the address as Viale Pietro Canonica (Piazza di Siena) 2, 00197 Roma, with the Roma Capitale call centre on 060608, daily 09.00 to 19.00. Winter hours, from the last Sunday of October to the last Saturday of March, are Tuesday to Sunday 10.00 to 16.00, with last admission at 15.15, an hour earlier if the visit takes in the private apartment on the first floor and the Villa Borghese sculpture store; 24 and 31 December are 10.00 to 14.00 and 1 January 2026 is 11.00 to 16.00. Summer hours, from the last Sunday of March to the last Saturday of October, are Tuesday to Friday 10.00 to 16.00 and Saturday and Sunday 10.00 to 19.00, with last admission forty-five minutes before closing and an hour earlier for the apartment and the store. It is closed on Mondays, 1 May and 25 December. Tickets are 7.50 euro full and 6.00 euro reduced, or 11.00 and 7.50 when an exhibition is running, with a presale charge of 1.00 euro online and none at the desk; the MIC card at 5.00 euro gives twelve months' free entry across the civic museums. The private apartment and the sculpture store are visitable in museum hours, accompanied by room staff.
places.history: Seventeenth-century documents call the building the Gallinaro, where ostriches, peacocks and ducks were raised for the Borghese family's hunts. Its present name comes from the medieval-looking turreted enclosure added in the late eighteenth century and attributed to Antonio Asprucci. Felice Giani decorated the facade with eight caryatid heads over the doors and windows in 1793. In 1919, when it was in use as administrative offices, a fire led to its abandonment. In 1926 it was given over to the sculptor Pietro Canonica, who fitted out the building and turned the stables into exhibition rooms; after his death in 1959 the collection of his works formed the first nucleus of the museum, and his widow, who died in 1987, left the comune the furnishings of the apartment they had lived in. In the courtyard stands a fifteenth-century octagonal well-head carrying Cardinal Rangoni's arms, from one of the demolished cloisters of Santa Maria in Aracoeli and moved here in 1960, and a white-marble mascaron fountain on the east wall.

places.name: Museo Carlo Bilotti - Aranciera di Villa Borghese
places.summary: A civic museum in the Aranciera of Villa Borghese. The museum's own contact page gives two addresses side by side, Via Fiorello La Guardia 6 and Viale dell'Aranciera 4, 00197 Roma, with the email info@museocarlobilotti.it and the call centre on 060608. It opens Tuesday to Friday 10.00 to 16.00 and Saturday and Sunday 10.00 to 19.00, with last admission forty-five minutes before closing; 24 and 31 December are 10.00 to 14.00 and 1 January 2026 is 11.00 to 16.00; it is closed on Mondays, 1 May and 25 December. Tickets follow the civic-museum tariff of 7.50 euro full and 6.00 euro reduced, or 11.00 and 7.50 with an exhibition, and the MIC card is 5.00 euro. The collection includes work by Giorgio de Chirico, among it Cavalli in riva al mare, Archeologi misteriosi, Autoritratto con testa di Minerva, Donna bionda di spalle, Cavaliere antico and Cavallo, together with Andy Warhol's Madre e figlia: Tina e Lisa Bilotti, Larry Rivers's Carlo con Dubuffet sullo sfondo, and works by Gino Severini and Giacomo Manzu.
places.history: The building is the Aranciera, the Casino dei giuochi d'acqua remodelled for Marcantonio IV Borghese by Antonio Asprucci from 1766. In the atrium and to the left of the building, at Piazzale Victor Hugo, are two seventeenth-century features: a rustic nymphaeum with a sarcophagus, and a tufa rockwork fountain.

places.name: Casa del Cinema
places.summary: A cinema and cultural venue in the Casina delle Rose inside Villa Borghese, at Largo Marcello Mastroianni 1. It has three screening and conference rooms, an open-air theatre for digital projection and live performance, two exhibition rooms, a networking space, a cafeteria and a restaurant. The outdoor arena is the Teatro all'aperto Ettore Scola, part of this venue rather than a separate one.
places.history: The idea came from the journalist Felice Laudadio. The Casina delle Rose, comune property and derelict for twenty-five years, was identified in September 2001, restored for seven million euro and inaugurated by the mayor Walter Veltroni on 18 September 2004. Laudadio directed it until 2011, Caterina D'Amico from 2011 to 2014 and Giorgio Gosetti from 2014 to 2022. Management passed from the Azienda Speciale Palaexpo to Zetema in February 2011 and to the Fondazione Cinema per Roma in February 2023; after a restyling it reopened on 5 May 2023, with the editorial line curated by Paola Malanga.

places.name: Cinema dei Piccoli
places.summary: A cinema of 71.52 square metres and sixty-three seats inside Villa Borghese, with a screen five metres by two and a half. Its own site gives the address as Viale della Pineta 15, 00197 Roma and the telephone number +39 06 8553485. No standard ticket price is published.
places.history: Alfredo Annibali built it in 1934 as the Casa di Topolino, with a Mickey Mouse holding a cine-camera beside the sign until Disney forced the name off, the image staying until the 1970s; it shut during the war and reopened straight after. At the end of the 1970s the programming passed to Enzo Fiorenza, founder of AIACE, who opened it to art cinema; in 1978 AIACE gave it to Fulvio Wetzl and Titta Labonia, who founded the Piccolo Officine cineclub and gave Wenders's Falso movimento its Italian premiere. Roberto Fiorenza and Caterina Roverso have run it since 1980; it ran a schools programme with the Cineteca Nazionale from 1993 to 1995, and the Dei Piccoli Film Festival began in 2007 with support from the Regione Lazio. DTS stereo and the present screen came with the 1991 refit, a Sony 4K projector in 2013 and a Barco SP 2K-7 laser projector in 2021.

places.name: Gigi Proietti Globe Theatre Silvano Toti
places.summary: A circular timber theatre on the Elizabethan model, at Largo Aqua Felix inside Villa Borghese, near Piazza di Siena, which stages a summer Shakespeare season. It seats 1,206 in all, with a standing pit for up to 415 and boxes on three levels linked by walkways; it is ten metres high, twenty-three metres across inside and thirty-three metres outside, with an external circumference of a hundred metres. It is built entirely in oak from managed and replanted forest, with a floor of dry-laid tufa blocks and a copper-shingle roof.
places.history: The comune built it in 2003, in three months, from an idea of Gigi Proietti's and with finance from the Fondazione Silvano Toti, and it opened that year with Romeo e Giulietta directed by Proietti, who was artistic director for seventeen years until his death in 2020. On 3 November 2020 the mayor Virginia Raggi and the foundation announced that it would also carry Proietti's name. Nicola Piovani became artistic director in the summer of 2022. An archive was opened in 2020 with the foreign-languages department of Roma Tre. On the morning of 22 September 2022, at the end of a morning performance of Macbeth, the stair of the theatre's outermost ring collapsed and twelve people were injured, five adults and seven young people aged between fifteen and nineteen, most of them pupils of the Liceo Saffo of Roseto degli Abruzzi on a school trip; the theatre was sequestered for the investigation and the repairs, and the 2023 season played in an adjacent temporary arena of 860 seats.

places.name: Casina di Raffaello
places.address: Via della Casina di Raffaello, 00197 Roma RM
places.summary: Villa Borghese's playroom, for children from three to fourteen, with a separate area for under-threes. Roma Capitale's tourism service gives the seasonal calendar. In winter, November to February, it opens Tuesday to Friday 10.00 to 15.30 and Saturdays, Sundays and holidays 10.00 to 18.00. In spring and autumn, March to 8 June and 15 September to October, it opens Tuesday to Friday 10.00 to 18.00 and Saturdays, Sundays and holidays 10.00 to 19.00. In summer, 5 June to 30 August, it opens Monday to Friday 08.30 to 17.30 and Saturday 10.00 to 15.00. It runs 10.00 to 14.00 on 24 and 31 December, and closes on Mondays, 1 January, Easter Monday, 1 May, 25 December and from 9 to 23 August.
places.history: The name misleads, and the sources say so: it has nothing to do with Raffaello Sanzio, who neither designed the building nor lived in it, and the confusion is with the Casino di Raffaello that stood at Villa Doria in the Galoppatoio. It was built in the seventeenth century for Cardinal Scipione Borghese at the same time as the Villa Pinciana, standing in a mulberry grove that was felled when Piazza di Siena was made, from which came its first name, the Palazzina dell'arboreto de' gelsi. It began as the villa wardrobe-keeper's lodging, with two loggias, one decorated in chiaroscuro; the small square garden beside it, with an orchard and a citrus grove, was replaced in the eighteenth century under the Asprucci by the church of Santa Maria Immacolata. It stayed a private residence until 2003. The restoration reinstated the eighteenth-century arrangement given it by Antonio Asprucci, and the principal ground-floor room carries frescoes by Felice Giani.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria Immacolata a Villa Borghese
places.summary: A small church on Piazza di Siena, set within the Casina di Raffaello, with a portico of four Doric columns. It is a subsidiary place of worship of the parish of Santa Teresa d'Avila.
places.history: It was made at the end of the eighteenth century for Prince Marcantonio Borghese, who had a farmworkers' casale on his land converted into a church, the work entrusted to Mario Asprucci. Felice Giani frescoed it between 1791 and 1793; the infobox of its own article gives 1792 as the start of building. Pietro Carrarini did further work and frescoes in 1829.

places.name: Piazza di Siena
places.summary: A wide oval arena inside Villa Borghese, closed to vehicles, between viale Pietro Canonica and viale dei Pupazzi. It is named for Siena, where the Borghese family came from.
places.history: Prince Marcantonio IV Borghese, who lived from 1730 to 1800, asked for a space inside the villa that would recall piazza del Campo; the villa's own monument table dates it to 1792, and it was finished after his death and given over to public entertainments. Its track of 370.30 metres hosted the Italian athletics championships of 1907, 1908 and 1909. From 1922 it became the home of an equestrian competition, international from 1926, now the Concorso ippico internazionale Piazza di Siena, which reached its ninetieth edition in 2023. In 1960 it staged the individual jumping, the individual dressage and the individual and team eventing of the XVII Olympiad, with temporary stands for 15,000 spectators. Claudio Baglioni closed his Ale-oo tour here in 1982, and Renato Zero played eight Sei Zero concerts between 29 September and 9 October 2010.

places.name: Giardino del Lago
places.summary: The lake garden at the heart of Villa Borghese, with an artificial islet in the middle of the water carrying the Tempietto di Esculapio. Roma Capitale's own page records that boats can be hired on the lake, and names the Meridiana and the Fontana della Famiglia dei Satiri along the banks. The planting is subtropical and Mediterranean together, with trachycarpus, chamaerops and phoenix palms, stone pine, cypress, atlas cedar and cedar of Lebanon, swamp cypress, bamboo, magnolia, paulownia and eucalyptus; the recorded birds include peregrine falcon, kestrel, black kite, cormorant, moorhen and mallard.
places.history: Antonio Asprucci laid the garden out in 1786 for Marcantonio IV Borghese. The rustic lake dates from 1791 and a niche fountain from 1620. The Fontana dei Mascheroni e Tritoni of 1909 reuses sculpture brought from Piazza Navona. The Fonte Gaia at the centre of the lake, also called the fountain of the satyrs or of the rabbits, dates from 1929 and is a bronze group of two satyrs holding a young satyr.

places.name: Tempio di Esculapio
places.summary: An Ionic tempietto of 1786 standing on the islet in the middle of the Giardino del Lago, and the building the hired boats are rowed around.
places.history: It was built in 1786 as part of Antonio Asprucci's laying out of the lake garden for Marcantonio IV Borghese.

places.name: Tempio di Diana
places.address: Viale della Casina di Raffaello, 00197 Roma RM
places.summary: A monopteral tempietto of 1789 on viale della Casina di Raffaello, one of the garden buildings put up for the Borghese in the late eighteenth century.
places.history: Villa Borghese's own monument table dates it to 1789.

places.name: Tempio di Antonino e Faustina (Villa Borghese)
places.address: Viale di Antonino e Faustina, 00197 Roma RM
places.summary: A garden folly of 1792 on the avenue named after it, built deliberately as a ruin in the English taste, with two altars carrying Greek inscriptions on either side. It shares its name with the Forum temple in the rione Campitelli and is a different building.
places.history: Cristoforo Unterperger designed it for Marcantonio Borghese in 1792, assembling ancient fragments to make a ruin.

places.name: Arco di Settimio Severo (Villa Borghese)
places.summary: A nineteenth-century folly at Largo Santander, at the entrance to the Giardino del Lago, built in the Roman manner with a statue of the emperor Septimius Severus on top. It is not an ancient monument, and it is not the Forum arch of the same name in the rione Campitelli.
places.history: Luigi Canina designed it and placed the emperor's statue at its summit.

places.name: Propilei Egizi
places.address: Viale Fiorello La Guardia, 00197 Roma RM
places.summary: A pair of Egyptian-style propylaea of 1825 on viale Fiorello La Guardia, built to join the Muro Torto gardens to the avenue on which they stand.
places.history: Luigi Canina built them in 1825 in an Egyptian manner.

places.name: Portico dei Leoni
places.address: Viale Fiorello La Guardia, 00197 Roma RM
places.summary: A columned portico on viale Fiorello La Guardia, in the taste of its period, begun in the late eighteenth century and finished in the early nineteenth.
places.history: Antonio Asprucci began it and Luigi Canina finished it.

places.name: Grotta dei Vini
places.summary: A seventeenth-century grotto near the via Pinciana entrance to the park, used by the Borghese for parties and banquets and as a wine cellar. Its vault carries frescoes set among stuccoes with pagan mythological subjects.
places.history: It was built to a design by Flaminio Ponzio, and Archita Ricci designed the decoration of the vault.

places.name: Serbatoio dell'Acqua Marcia
places.summary: A water reservoir in a baroque manner standing in the Parco dei Daini, built between 1922 and 1925 to serve the surrounding quartieri.
places.history: Raffaele De Vico designed it between 1922 and 1925. It held the supply of the Acqua Pia Antica Marcia that fed the villa's fountains and lakes, water now brought from the Peschiera.

places.name: Uccelliera, Meridiana e Giardini Segreti di Villa Borghese
places.summary: Two small seventeenth-century pavilions, the Uccelliera and the Meridiana, standing beside the Galleria Borghese with the enclosed gardens between them. Roma Capitale names four: the Giardino dell'Uccelliera, the Giardino Vecchio, the Giardino della Meridiana and the Giardino della Coltivazione, restored from historical and iconographic documentation, and the Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that they were brought back to their original seventeenth-century arrangement.
places.history: The gardens hold two eighteenth-century fountains carrying Borghese heraldry, the Fontana dell'Aquila in the first secret garden and the Fontana del Drago in the second, together with four rustic fountainlets in marmo africano of 1609 to 1623 in the second and third gardens, and a circular fountain at the fourth, on viale dell'Uccelliera.

places.name: Casino del Graziano
places.address: Viale del Giardino Zoologico, 00197 Roma RM
places.summary: A three-storey casino on viale del Giardino Zoologico, at the edge of the Valle dei Platani, the third floor a loggia room. Inside its enclosure wall are two square courtyards, each with a rockwork fountain, and the ground floor carries sixteenth-century grotesque decoration including a Rape of Europa in the manner of Prospero Fontana.
places.history: It was built in the sixteenth century for one Stefano Graziani. Cardinal Borghese bought it in 1616 meaning to show pictures and statues in it, but used it mainly as a place of pleasure and rest after hunting.

places.name: Casale Cenci-Giustiniani
places.summary: A farmhouse on viale David Lubin whose facades and portico carry fresco fragments of sculpture and trompe-l'oeil perspectives. It now houses a cultural association.
places.history: It appears as a dependency of the Orti Giustiniani on a plan of 1828 and as the Casale Giustinani in an engraving by G. H. Busse of 1840.

places.name: Parco dei Daini
places.summary: An enclosed quarter of Villa Borghese, named by both the Sovrintendenza Capitolina and Roma Capitale among the places of the park, planted with holm oak, bay, black poplar, red oak, hackberry, stone pine, cypress and olive. It holds the Edicola del Dace, an early twentieth-century aedicule with a Hadrianic statue of a Dacian, and the Acqua Marcia reservoir.
places.history: Raffaele De Vico made the small artificial lake between 1922 and 1925, with a concrete silenus at its centre, the Fontana con Sileno che versa l'acqua, also called the fountain of Atlas.

places.name: Valle dei Platani
places.address: Viale del Giardino Zoologico, 00197 Roma RM
places.summary: A wooded valley in the northern part of Villa Borghese, planted with oriental plane, lime, common and black walnut, catalpa, albizia, hackberry, red and pedunculate oak, sweet chestnut, box elder, black locust, horse chestnut and Judas tree.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that the ground was brought into the villa under Giovanni Vasanzio, together with the land the Bioparco now occupies, to make a barco for hunting.

places.name: Giardini di Valle Giulia e Scalinata
places.address: Viale delle Belle Arti, 00197 Roma RM
places.summary: The gardens and the flight of steps that link Villa Borghese down to Valle Giulia and the museums on viale delle Belle Arti. On the steps stand the two Fontane delle Tartarughe di Valle Giulia, at the Esedra Petar II Petrovic Njegos and the Esedra Giulio Carlo Argan. They are a different work from the Fontana delle Tartarughe in piazza Mattei, in the rione Sant'Angelo.
places.history: Cesare Bazzani designed the two Fontane delle Tartarughe di Valle Giulia in 1910 and they were built for the 1911 Esposizione nazionale; they were restored, together with the squares around them, in 2004.

places.name: Ingressi monumentali di Villa Borghese
places.summary: Six monumental gateways survive around Villa Borghese. The Portale Flaminio Ponzio of 1609 is on via Pinciana near number 67, arched and armorial, built by Flaminio Ponzio as the main entrance and moved back between 1910 and 1912 when via Pinciana was widened. The Propilei delle aquile of 1790, by Antonio Asprucci, first stood at the Muro Torto entrance and were moved to Porta Pinciana in 1933; they now front piazzale San Paolo del Brasile. The Propilei neoclassici, completed in 1827 by Luigi Canina on ancient Greek models, stand at piazzale Flaminio. The seventeenth-century Portale del leone on via P. Raimondi, attributed to Flaminio Ponzio, keeps its lion protome above the keystone and gives on to the Parco dei Daini. The Portale del drago of 1617 on via Pinciana carries the Borghese dragon under a pediment. The Portale dei vasi was moved in 1914 from Porta Pinciana to the entrance of the zoological garden on via Ulisse Aldrovandi.
places.history: The gates belong to two campaigns: the Borghese building of the early seventeenth century, under Flaminio Ponzio, and the remodelling of the park under Antonio Asprucci and then Luigi Canina between the 1790s and the 1820s, when Camillo Borghese extended the grounds toward porta del Popolo and porta Pinciana.

places.name: Fontana dei Cavalli Marini
places.address: Piazzale dei Cavalli Marini, 00197 Roma RM
places.summary: A fountain of 1791 at the piazzale that takes its name, a large circular basin carried on four hippocamps.
places.history: The painter Cristopher Unterberger designed it on an earlier model and Vincenzo Pacetti executed it. It replaced, in the eighteenth century, an earlier fountain called del Mascherone.

places.name: Fontana del Fiocco
places.summary: Also called the Fontana di Esculapio, a classical arch with a statue of Aesculapius in it, at Piazza del Fiocco.
places.history: Luigi Canina designed it and it was built between 1830 and 1834, during the works that joined the Borghese grounds to Piazza del Popolo; the villa's own table gives 1833 in one column and the range in another.

places.name: Fontana dei Pupazzi
places.summary: A late eighteenth-century fountain on viale dei Pupazzi, at Piazza di Siena, whose granite basin appears to come from an earlier fountain of Narcissus that stood behind the Casino Nobile.
places.history: The putti and dolphins that gave the fountain its name were stolen in 1983.

places.name: Mostra dell'Acqua Felice (Villa Borghese)
places.summary: A late eighteenth-century water display on viale Pietro Canonica: a sarcophagus slab carried by two griffins and surmounted by a lion, with a shell-shaped fountainlet on either side.
places.history: Antonio Asprucci built it. It takes its name from the Acqua Felice, whose aqueduct works for the villa were entrusted to Giovanni Fontana in 1610.

places.name: Le altre fontane di Villa Borghese
places.summary: Villa Borghese holds some fifty fountains, most of them a name, a century and an avenue. The Fontane Oscure, formerly the Fontana Rotonda and the Fontana Ovale, of 1620, face each other across viale del Museo Borghese. Two shell-basin fountainlets of 1618 to 1620 stand at Piazzale Scipione Borghese, with a nineteenth-century Seconda Fontana della Venere; two trilobed fountainlets with reliefs of about 1897 are at Piazzale Museo Borghese. The two Fontane delle Piramidi, of the late seventeenth century, are on viale delle Piramidi, and the Fontana di Diana and the Prima Fontana della Venere are in the Italian gardens at Piazzale Ferdowsi. The Fontana del Sarcofago delle Vittorie of 1917 is on viale Goethe. On viale Fiorello La Guardia are the Fontana dei Leoni, made before 1788, and the oval-basin fountain of the Preschiera of 1908, built when the bridge linking Villa Borghese to the Pincio was made. On viale Giorgio Washington are a sixteenth-century fountain-nymphaeum with a small lake and a headless river god, both of which came from the Villa Giustiniani.
places.history: In 1610 the construction of the Acqua Felice aqueduct and the villa's fountains was entrusted to Giovanni Fontana. Raffaele De Vico later built the reservoir of the Acqua Pia Antica Marcia that supplied the fountains and the lakes, water now brought from the Peschiera.

places.name: I monumenti donati di Villa Borghese
places.summary: Foreign states and associations have given Villa Borghese a long series of statues, standing along the avenues around Piazzale Ferdowsi and Viale Madama Letizia. In date order: Wolfgang Goethe, 1904, on viale Goethe, in Carrara marble by Valentino Casali, given by Wilhelm II of Germany, with three groups at the base for the dramatic, lyric and didactic strands of Goethe's poetics, Iphigenia and Orestes, Mignon and Lothario, and Faust and Mephistopheles; Victor Hugo, 1905, at Piazzale Victor Hugo, by Lucien Pallez, given by the Franco-Italian League; Umberto I, on viale della Pineta, begun by Davide Calandra in 1914, completed by Edoardo Rubino and inaugurated in 1926, a bronze equestrian statue on a porphyry base with reliefs of Valour and royal Piety and a veiled Italia mourning the king; the Alpino and the Umile Eroe, on viale Pietro Canonica in front of the Museo Canonica, where Pietro Canonica gave his bronze of the mule Scudela in 1940 and the Alpino was added in 1957; George Byron, about 1959, on via della Pineta, a copy after Bertel Thorvaldsen's statue at Trinity College, Cambridge, with passages from Childe Harold's Pilgrimage on the pedestal; Ferdowsi, 1958, by Sadighi, in marble, given by the city of Tehran; Francisco de Paula Santander, 1961, by Carlos Viejo, given by Colombia; Ahmed Shawqi, 1962, by Gamal El Sagini, given by Cairo's higher council for literature, arts and sciences; Jose Artigas, 1966, a copy after Jose L. Zorilla, given by the Italo-Uruguayan association; Garcilaso de la Vega, 1967, by Joaquin Roca Rey, given by the Peruvian committee; Aleksandr Pushkin, 2000, by Yuri Orekow, given by the city of Moscow; Nikolaj Gogol, 2002, by Zurab Tsereteli, given by Russia; Petar Njegos, 2005, a copy after Sreten Stojanovic, given by Montenegro; Henryk Sienkiewicz, 2006, by Czeslaw Dzwigaj, for the Archconfraternity of Archers of Krakow with the Polish embassy's patronage, replacing an earlier Sienkiewicz; and Nizami Ganjavi, 2012, by Salxab Mammadov and Ali Ibadullayev, given by Azerbaijan. There are also a stele to Jose Marti and Garibaldi of 1983 on Viale Madama Letizia and a stele to George Washington of 2000 on Viale Giorgio Washington.
places.history: Two of the series need a note. Pietro Canonica's Simon Bolivar is dated by the monument's own table to 1930, placed originally at what is now piazzale Manila and moved in 1960; Pinciano's own article dates the bronze 1933 and puts it originally in the viale Tiziano gardens. The two accounts are not reconciled here. Giuseppe Ceracchi's eighteenth-century monument to Jan van der Capellen de Poll, made for the Netherlands, was bought by the Borghese in 1835 and divided into four parts, Capellen de Poll in Roman dress and allegories of Temperance and Justice with a lion for Fortitude; it is in deposit at the Museo Pietro Canonica and is not on display where it stood.

places.name: Valle Giulia
places.address: Viale delle Belle Arti, 00197 Roma RM
places.summary: A small valley between Villa Borghese and the Parioli hill, still holding Villa Giulia, and the address of a cluster of foreign research institutes. Its present layout comes largely from the 1911 national exposition, for which Cesare Bazzani's Galleria Nazionale was built; from 1911 onward, and through the decades that followed, foreign countries sited their institutes here. Villa Elia, on via di San Valentino, is the seat of the embassy of Portugal to the Holy See.
places.history: On the slopes facing the valley is the faculty of architecture that La Sapienza inaugurated in 1920 and that is still there. On 1 March 1968 the area around the faculty was the scene of serious clashes between students and police, which came to be called the battle of Valle Giulia and about which Pier Paolo Pasolini wrote Il PCI ai giovani!.

places.name: British School at Rome
places.summary: A residential research institute in Valle Giulia, at Via Antonio Gramsci 61, 00197 Roma, in a building by Edwin Lutyens. It publishes events, exhibitions and a library rather than general opening hours, so none are given here. Its director is Abigail Brundin. Piazzale Simon Bolivar, with the monument to Bolivar, is in front of it.
places.history: It was founded in 1901 and recognised by Royal Charter in 1912. Lutyens designed the building as the British pavilion of the 1911 international exposition in Rome, taking the upper storey of St Paul's Cathedral in London as his model; the Italian state then gave the land, and the permanent building was completed in 1916.

places.name: Istituto Giapponese di Cultura
places.summary: Japan's cultural institute in Rome, on via Antonio Gramsci in Valle Giulia. A Japanese garden is part of the institute. No source states the garden's opening times, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states an institutional history of the institute.

places.name: Accademia di Danimarca
places.summary: Denmark's academy in Rome, which gives its address in its own footer as Via Omero 18, 00197 Roma, among the foreign institutes of Valle Giulia. No opening hours are published for it, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states an institutional history of the academy.

places.name: Forum Austriaco di Cultura
places.summary: Austria's cultural forum in Rome, which gives its address on its own site as Viale Bruno Buozzi 113, 00197 Roma. No opening hours are published for it, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states an institutional history of the forum.

places.name: Gli istituti stranieri di Valle Giulia
places.summary: Four more foreign research institutes stand in Valle Giulia: the Reale Istituto Neerlandese, or KNIR, of the Koninklijke Nederlandse Akademie van Wetenschappen; the Academia Belgica; the Istituto svedese di studi classici; and the Accademia di Romania. They are named as institutes of the valley by the source for Valle Giulia itself. No street numbers are given for them here, and no opening hours.
places.history: The siting of foreign research institutes in Valle Giulia began with the 1911 national exposition and continued through the decades that followed.

places.name: Chiesa della Madonna dell'Arco Oscuro
places.address: Viale delle Belle Arti, 00197 Roma RM
places.summary: A two-room chapel cut into the tufa on viale delle Belle Arti, near Villa Giulia. The first room is modern, with ex-votos and a mosaic Annunciation; the second is the late eighteenth-century chapel proper, holding the arco oscuro itself with the Marian image walled in, and a Via Crucis of fourteen stations. A plaque outside reads Sacellum Matri Divinae Providentiae de Arcu Obscuro dicatum, and the arms of Innocent XI are on the entrance architrave.
places.history: It was built in 1797 and consecrated on 10 September of that year, to house a Marian icon that had hung under the bridge linking Villa Poniatowski to Villa Giulia, the dark arch that gives the church its name. The Giornale di Roma of 30 September 1797 records Fra Giovanni Andrea Michelotti chiselling the chapel out of the tufa and its solemn blessing on the Sunday.

places.name: Basilica di Sant'Eugenio
places.address: Viale delle Belle Arti, 00197 Roma RM
places.summary: A neo-baroque parish church on viale delle Belle Arti, with a travertine facade of two orders, one tall central portal and two lower side ones, six pilasters with eclectic Corinthian capitals, Alessandro Monteleone's allegories of Justice and Peace over the minor portals, Francesco Nagni's symbols of the four Evangelists flanking the loggia window above, and a bronze St Michael by A. Gerardi on the dome. The bell tower behind carries eight bells in B flat, cast by the Fonderia Colbachini of Padua in the 1950s. Inside are three aisles on paired columns, a transept, five side chapels and a high dome.
places.history: As the twenty-fifth anniversary of Pius XII's episcopal consecration approached, the pope let it be known that he wished to use the gifts promised to him by Catholics around the world to build a church in a new Roman quarter that had no parish church. It was dedicated to St Eugene I, Pacelli's baptismal name. Work began in 1942 to designs by Enrico Pietro Galeazzi and Mario Redini, was interrupted by the war and finished in 1951, and Pius XII consecrated the church himself on 2 June 1951. The parish was erected in 1951 by the brief Petrianae navis of 16 March; it has been a cardinalatial deaconry since 1960 and has been served by priests of the personal prelature of Opus Dei since 1980. The brief Honoris pastoralis raised it to minor basilica on 23 May 1951, which the source dates before the consecration; both dates are reported as given. John Paul II visited on 3 March 1986.

places.name: Basilica di Santa Teresa d'Avila
places.summary: A neo-Romanesque church at Corso d'Italia 37, belonging with its attached curia generalizia to the Discalced Carmelites and dedicated to their Spanish foundress. The campanile is forty metres high, with blind arcading and a clock. The facade has two orders: below, a portal with a protiro on columns and a pediment; above, a small loggia of arches and colonnettes, and between two pilaster strips whose bases carry two marble lions by Armando Brasini, a rose window with Christ and the apostles under a cross-shaped window. The Carmelite Serafino Melchiorre made the bronze panels of episodes from the life of St Teresa in the doorway, with a relief of Christ blessing and St Teresa in the lunette. Inside are three aisles on piers and arches under a groin vault, confessionals by the cabinetmaker Alfonsi and a marble pulpit carved with scenes from the saint's life.
places.history: It was built between 1901 and 1902 to designs by Tullio Passarelli, who carried out most of the later remodelling himself, and inaugurated on 20 April 1902, as a plaque left of the main door records. Pius X erected the parish on 6 January 1906 by the bull Romanas aequabilis; Pius XII raised the church to minor basilica in 1951; and it has been a cardinalatial title, Santa Teresa al corso d'Italia, since 1962. The side aisles were raised above the central one until 1936.

places.name: Basilica del Sacro Cuore Immacolato di Maria
places.summary: The church that closes piazza Euclide, on a Greek-cross plan inscribed in a circle behind an elaborate facade. No opening hours are published for it, so none are given here.
places.history: Pinciano's own article dates the church to the twentieth century, between 1923 and 1951. it.wikipedia gives Armando Brasini as its architect, records the consecration of the crypt in 1936, and records that John XXIII raised the church to minor basilica in May 1959 and that Paul VI made it a titular church in February 1965.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Teresa del Bambin Gesu in Panfilo
places.summary: A church at the junction of via Giovanni Paisiello and via Gaspare Spontini, and the reason it matters to a visitor is underground: the present access to the catacomb of San Panfilo is inside it. No opening hours are published for the church, so none are given here.
places.history: it.wikipedia gives Guglielmo Palombi as the architect, dates the building between 1929 and 1932 and the consecration to 2 October 1932, and records that the church was a parish church from 6 December 1952, by a decree of Cardinal Clemente Micara, until 30 September 2011. It was built over the catacomb, whose tunnels carry pilgrim graffiti and funerary inscriptions.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria della Pace ai Parioli
places.summary: The prelatic church of Opus Dei, on viale Bruno Buozzi. Its name says Parioli and its own article says the quartiere Pinciano. The remains of the founder, St Josemaria Escriva de Balaguer, who lived from 1902 to 1975, are in the altar. The font is the one in which he was baptised in 1902, given to the church by the diocese of Barbastro. In the crypt are Blessed Alvaro del Portillo, bishop and first successor, 1914 to 1994, Javier Echevarria Rodriguez, 1932 to 2016, and Dora del Hoyo, 1914 to 2004; in the sub-crypt is Carmen Escriva, the founder's sister. OpenStreetMap gives the street number as 75; no other source consulted carries one, so the number is reported as an aggregator's figure rather than stated here.
places.history: No source gives a construction date or an architect for the church, and none is given here.

places.name: Mausoleo di Lucilio Peto
places.summary: A great circular tomb of the last years of the first century BC, on the west side of the via Salaria about 500 metres from the Aurelian Walls, its entrance on the road. The drum is about thirty-four metres across and sixteen metres high, a concrete core faced in travertine blocks between two plain dentil cornices, and the covering was probably a conical earth tumulus. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives it as temporarily closed.
places.history: It was discovered in 1887, about six metres below the modern level, during work on the former Vigna Bertone, and belongs to the burial ground along the via Salaria. The marble inscription on the main front, in Luni marble, of which five courses survive within a Lesbian cyma, assigns it to Lucilius Paetus of the Scaptia tribe, military tribune, prefect of engineers and of cavalry, who built it in his lifetime for himself and his sister Lucilia Polla. A rear entrance and corridor lead to a cruciform burial chamber with three niches for funerary couches. It was abandoned and almost buried by the Trajanic period, and reused in the fourth century, when small masonry tombs were built against the drum, two tiers of loculi were cut into the corridor, and a small catacomb with a main gallery and unused branches was dug into the tufa and reached by a stair. It was robbed of its furnishings and marble in the fourth century and again in the sixteenth and seventeenth. It reopened to the public in August 2010 after a long restoration campaign, and was restored again in 2025 under the PNRR Caput Mundi programme.

places.name: Ipogeo di via Livenza
places.summary: An underground late-antique hall between via Livenza and via Po, of which a trapezoidal fragment survives. Its north wall is articulated in three adjacent arches; the central one, richly frescoed and mosaicked and closed by two marble screens, holds a deep rectangular basin, 2.90 by 1.70 metres and 2.50 metres deep, with a water inlet and outlet and three steps down, the first of them very high, the stair keeping many of its original ancient treads. The building was about 21 by 7 metres, oriented north to south. A surviving mosaic fragment may show St Peter striking water from a rock to baptise a converted centurion. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina states that the site is temporarily closed to the public for works under the PNRR. Its published terms for when it opens are accompanied groups only, a maximum of ten people per visit, booking obligatory on 060608 between 09.00 and 19.00, and tickets at 4.00 euro full and 3.00 euro reduced, free for residents of Rome and the metropolitan area on production of proof of residence and for MIC card holders, with guided tours not included in the price.
places.history: The hypogeum was found in 1923, when the digging for a small block of flats between via Livenza and via Po brought an underground building to light and damaged its structures beyond repair. It is dated by consensus to the second half of the fourth century AD, and what it was for is still argued: a shrine of the Thracian goddess Cotys and the mystery sect of the Baptai, an early baptistery, a temple of a water cult, a place of magical practice, a meeting place for a syncretistic sect, or a nymphaeum built over an underground spring. It was restored in 2025 under the PNRR Caput Mundi programme.

places.name: Catacomba di San Panfilo
places.summary: A catacomb running under via Paisiello and via Spontini, in the care of the Pontificia Commissione di Archeologia Sacra, on the line of the ancient Salaria vetus; ancient sources call it the first catacomb on that road out of porta Pinciana. The present access is inside the church of Santa Teresa del Bambin Gesu in Panfilo. It has three levels, a lower and an upper joined together with an intermediate one between them. The lower, twenty metres below ground, dates from the third century, with a main artery like an underground decumanus about sixty metres long and galleries at right angles to it. No source states hours or access, so none are given here.
places.history: A new region of galleries was added at the lower level in the fourth century, containing the cubiculum duplex in which the remains of the martyr Pamphilus, of Carthaginian origin, were found. The intermediate level is essentially two ambulacra joined by galleries; the upper, badly damaged by the buildings above it, is dated between 348 and 361. The primitive nucleus is third-century. The catacomb was forgotten after the catacombs were abandoned; Antonio Bosio entered the first level on 16 May 1594, after which it stayed hidden from the relic-hunters for three more centuries, which is why the two lower levels survive; Enrico Josi rediscovered and identified it from 1920.

places.name: Catacomba di Sant'Ermete
places.summary: A catacomb on the ancient Salaria vetus, today under via Bertoloni, in the care of the Pontificia Commissione di Archeologia Sacra. It is also called the catacomb of Bassilla. No source states whether or how it can be visited, so nothing is given here.
places.history: The older of its two names, Bassilla, belongs either to the owner of the ground in which the underground cemetery was dug in the first half of the third century or to the martyr whom the Depositio martyrum commemorates on 22 September, killed in Diocletian's persecution of 304; scholars have not settled it, and the source says a case of homonymy cannot be excluded. Sant'Ermete is the martyr from whom the catacomb takes its other name. Early liturgical sources record four burials on the Salaria vetus, Ermete, Proto, Giacinto and Bassilla, and early medieval pilgrim itineraries add Crispo, Ercolano, Leopardo, Vittore and Massimiliano, of whom almost nothing is known. The Notitia ecclesiarum urbis Romae attests a basilica above ground dedicated to Bassilla. Inscriptions of Bassilla from this catacomb are now in the Museo Pio Cristiano in Vatican City.

places.name: Porta Pinciana
places.summary: One of the gates of the Aurelian Walls, standing at piazzale Brasile, where Corso d'Italia ends. Two semicircular flanking towers stand either side of the travertine arch. No visiting arrangements are published for it, so none are given here.
places.history: The gate was enlarged from an earlier posterula by the emperor Honorius during the restoration of 403, when the two semicircular flanking towers were added; the original travertine arch survives. It carried two earlier names: Porta Turata, because it had been walled up, and Porta Salaria Vetus, because the older via Salaria left the city here. A medieval story calls it the Porta Belisaria and has the general Belisarius begging at it; the source that reports the story says outright that it is false.

places.name: Mura Aureliane: il tratto da Porta Pinciana a piazza Fiume
places.summary: The stretch of the Aurelian Walls that runs east from Porta Pinciana as far as piazza Fiume, following Corso d'Italia, which was laid out along the outside of it. The walls are the southern edge of the quartiere here, with the rioni Ludovisi and Sallustiano on the far side. The named stretch to the west of Porta Pinciana, the Muro Torto, is in the rione Campo Marzio. No source states whether this stretch can be visited, so nothing is given here.
places.history: Porta Pinciana was enlarged by Honorius in 403.

places.name: Villa Strohl-Fern
places.summary: A walled estate of about 80,000 square metres on viale David Lubin, owned by the French state, laid out as a park of artists' studios in the nineteenth century. The Liceo Chateaubriand, the French lycee of Rome, is inside it.
places.history: It is named for the Alsatian patron and artist Alfred Wilhelm Strohl, born at Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines in 1847 and died in Rome in 1927, who took refuge in Paris during the war of 1870, travelled Europe and settled in Rome in 1879, buying eight hectares that year and turning them into a park of studios for artists of any school or nationality; the name joins his surname to the German word fern. Antonello Trombadori, who went there from 1919 with his father the painter Francesco Trombadori, wrote that the property had never been part of Villa Borghese but was a wooded and meadowed holding bordering it, running from the left propylaeum to the Valle Giulia steps, and that only after the Second World War was the park temporarily annexed to the public Villa Borghese while keeping its own history and identity. He described its core as a forbidden city behind a high fence, a fabulous garden of rare species with false-stalactite fountains, concrete tanks, cedars, bamboo and holm oaks. Francesco Trombadori had his studio there and died there in 1961.

places.name: Villa Lubin
places.summary: A neo-baroque and liberty building inside Villa Borghese, also called Villa Italia or the Palazzina Internazionale dell'Agricoltura, owned by the Italian state and the seat of the Consiglio nazionale dell'economia e del lavoro. In the access road below it is a grotto with a headless recumbent river god. No visiting information is published for it, so none is given here.
places.history: Pompeo Passerini designed it with Raffaele De Vico and it was built between 1906 and 1908 to house the Istituto internazionale di agricoltura, the precursor of the FAO, at David Lubin's instigation; its construction caused controversy because old pines had to be felled for it. In 1933 Paolo Rossi De Paoli built the villino Ruffo on the neighbouring piazzale, restructured in 1981, which today holds the CNEL's library of more than 75,000 books, a conference room and the office of the Autorita garante per l'infanzia e l'adolescenza; the small pavilion was the seat of the Istituto per l'Oriente from 1952 to 1960. After the institute moved to the FAO the building reverted to the Italian government, and the CNEL was installed on 20 February 1958; Clemente Busiri Vici restored and enlarged it in 1959, and in 1960 it also became the seat of the Committee of Ministers for the Mezzogiorno. The building appears on the Italian 200-lire coin struck in 1981 for the first World Food Day.

places.name: Villa Balestra
places.summary: A public municipal garden of 15,000 square metres owned by the Comune di Roma, on the top of Monte San Valentino, the tufa hill above viale Tiziano. Its own article notes that although the garden occupies a spur of the Parioli hills it belongs to the quartiere Pinciano, as does via Bartolomeo Ammannati, by which it is reached.
places.history: It occupies a small part of the grounds of Villa Poggio, built by the Bolognese cardinal Giovanni Poggio, treasurer of the Apostolic Camera under Paul III and nuncio in Spain and Germany. An encyclopaedia of 1834 still calls it the villa Poggi outside Porta del Popolo, where cardinals and ambassadors halted when making their public entry into Rome. Cavaliere Giuseppe Balestra bought it in 1880 and returned the farmed part to vineyard. The estate was broken up from 1910 and part of it was built over in 1928.

places.name: Villa Marignoli
places.summary: An Art Nouveau villino on the corner of via Po, numbers 2 to 4, and Corso d'Italia, number 35. It was built as the Marignoli family's town residence and is now a residenza turistico-alberghiera.
places.history: Giulio Magni designed it in 1907. Magni was born at Velletri on 1 November 1859 and was a great-nephew of Giuseppe Valadier.

places.name: Villino Astaldi
places.summary: A villino on the corner of via Saverio Mercadante and via Niccolo Porpora, a rectangular main block along via Mercadante of two storeys over a semi-basement with an attic, and a smaller block behind.
places.history: It was built between 1920 and 1923 as the villino Rosmunda, for the daughter of the engineer Adolfo Sebastiani, on land bordering Villa Borghese subdivided after the master plan of 1909; Arnaldo Foschini designed it with Attilio Spaccarelli. A second campaign of 1955 to 1956 was by Mario Ridolfi and Volfango Frankl. The house was later associated with Maria Luisa Astaldi and with Italia Nostra.

places.name: Villino Alatri
places.summary: A villino at the crossing of via Giovanni Paisiello and via Vincenzo Bellini, entered from the latter. It has a right-angled corner front and an L-shaped plan with the long side on via Paisiello, where the entrance originally was, and an internal garden behind. There are three floors, two of them above ground; the basement holds the boiler, a garage and the porter's flat, and there is a third floor in the roof for the servants and an altana on the via Bellini side.
places.history: Giacomo Alatri, a textile manufacturer and a figure in the Roman Jewish community, commissioned it from Vittorio Ballio Morpurgo in the 1920s. Its own article dates it to 1928 and its restructuring to 1949; Pinciano's own article gives 1924 to 1928 and names no architect.

places.name: Villa Titta Ruffo
places.summary: A late liberty house at via Sassoferrato 11, also called the villino Titta Ruffo or villa Zanardo, built of tufa, grey stone and exposed brick, several heterogeneous blocks gathered around a five-storey central trunk with two square turrets, and terraces, loggias and altane in a Mediterranean vernacular. Its park keeps stone pines and tall palms.
places.history: It was built about 1919 as a single-family house for the baritone Titta Ruffo, to a design by the engineer Giovanni Sleiter, by the building firm of Zeffiro Rossellini, great-uncle of the director Roberto Rossellini.

places.name: Ex Istituto Cabrini
places.summary: A late nineteenth-century building on via Ulisse Aldrovandi in the barocchetto manner, built as the general house of the Missionarie del Sacro Cuore and long a girls' boarding school.
places.history: Pinciano's own article records that it was converted in 1981 into the Aldrovandi Villa Borghese hotel.

places.name: Villa Serena
places.summary: A neo-medieval house on via Carlo Dolci, made in 1909 out of an existing casino nobile.
places.history: The architect Garibaldi Burba carried out the conversion in 1909.

places.name: Palazzo dell'Istituto Poligrafico dello Stato
places.summary: An eclectic palazzo on piazza Giuseppe Verdi, built between 1913 and 1918 and the seat of the state printing institute until 2010.
places.history: Garibaldi Burba designed it, and it was built between 1913 and 1918.

places.name: Villa Ambron
places.address: Via delle Tre Madonne, Roma RM
places.summary: A house of 1920 on via delle Tre Madonne, in the barocchetto manner.
places.history: Marcello Piacentini designed it in 1920.

places.name: Palazzina Marchi
places.summary: A small apartment building of 1924 on via Giacomo Carissimi, in the barocchetto manner.
places.history: Mario Marchi designed it in 1924.

places.name: Palazzina Giorgi
places.summary: A small apartment building of 1927 on via Antonio Bertoloni, in the barocchetto manner.
places.history: The engineer Oscar Giorgi Alberti designed it in 1927.

places.name: Palazzina Virgili
places.summary: A rationalist apartment building of 1929 on via Angelo Secchi.
places.history: Pietro Aschieri designed it in 1929 for Filippo Virgili. In 1933 it became the residence of Benito Mussolini's daughter Edda and her husband Galeazzo Ciano.

places.name: Palazzina Acerbo
places.summary: A house of 1930 on via Nicolo Tartaglia, in the barocchetto manner, now the seat of the embassy of Venezuela. It is a working diplomatic mission on Italian soil; no visiting arrangements are published for it, so none are given here.
places.history: Guido Fiorini designed it in 1930 for Giacomo Acerbo.

places.name: Villa Giorgina
places.summary: A neoclassical villa of 1920 on via Po, the seat of the Apostolic Nunciature to Italy, a diplomatic mission standing on Italian soil. Its own article states that the building is not open to the public. The park around it covers 20,000 square metres and is enclosed by a wall running along via Po, via Salaria, largo Ponchielli, via Peri and via Caccini.
places.history: Clemente Busiri Vici designed it in 1920 for the industrialist and senator Isaia Levi, who named it for his daughter. Mussolini considered moving in in 1927 and declined because of the tram noise from via Po and via Salaria. Levi, a convert, left the villa to Pius XII in 1949, and John XXIII moved the nunciature's offices there ten years later, from a villa on via Nomentana now used by the Libyan embassy. Alberto Moravia set Gli indifferenti inside it and lived opposite as a child.

places.name: Palazzo Borromeo
places.address: Viale delle Belle Arti, 00197 Roma RM
places.summary: Palazzo Borromeo has housed Italy's embassy to the Holy See since 1929. It was built in 1561 to a design by Pirro Ligorio for Pius IV, is owned by the Italian state, and is not open to the public. It stands on Italian soil, on the via Flaminia frontage, with its entrance on via delle Belle Arti.
places.history: It was raised on Julius III's old vineyard, the same three vineyards that carry Villa Giulia and Villa Poniatowski, and it was built up against the pre-existing Fontana di papa Giulio III, which still faces the junction of via Flaminia and via di Villa Giulia. Its interiors carry stuccoes and frescoes commissioned by Pius IV and Marcantonio Colonna.

places.name: Fontana di papa Giulio III
places.address: Via di Villa Giulia, Roma RM
places.summary: A wall fountain by Bartolomeo Ammannati at the junction of via Flaminia and via di Villa Giulia, standing against the chamfered corner of the palazzetto of Pius IV.
places.history: It was fed by a conduit of the Aqua Virgo dug for Julius III's villa, the building that is now the Museo Nazionale Etrusco. Palazzo Borromeo was later built up against it.

places.name: Explora - Il Museo dei Bambini di Roma
places.summary: A children's museum on the east side of via Flaminia. Its own site gives the address in its footer as Via Flaminia 80/86, 00196 Roma. It admits Tuesday to Sunday in four sessions of an hour and three quarters, at 10.00 to 11.45, 12.00 to 13.45, 15.00 to 16.45 and 17.00 to 18.45, and is closed on Mondays.
places.history: No source states an institutional history of the museum.

entries.name: Villa Borghese
entries.note: Eighty hectares laid out for Scipione Borghese from 1606, bought by the state in 1901 and given to the comune in 1903; open daily from dawn to dusk, with nine gates.

entries.name: Galleria Borghese
entries.note: Scipione Borghese's collection in the casino built for it, with Bernini's David and Apollo e Dafne and Canova's Paolina Borghese; entry is by timed slot and no source states the hours.

entries.name: Museo Nazionale Etrusco di Villa Giulia
entries.note: Etruscan and Faliscan antiquities in Julius III's villa of 1551 to 1553, founded in 1889; Tuesday to Sunday 08.30 to 19.30, 13.00 euro full and 2.00 euro reduced.

entries.name: La Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea
entries.note: Cesare Bazzani's building for the 1911 exposition, open Tuesday to Sunday 08.30 to 19.30 at 10.00 euro full, with photography without flash permitted by its own rules.

entries.name: Museo Pietro Canonica a Villa Borghese
entries.note: The sculptor's museum in the Fortezzuola on Piazza di Siena, with his private apartment and the Villa Borghese sculpture store visitable in museum hours with a member of staff.

entries.name: Piazza di Siena
entries.note: The oval arena of 1792 that Marcantonio IV Borghese asked for in memory of piazza del Campo; it staged the Olympic jumping, dressage and eventing in 1960.

entries.name: Giardino del Lago
entries.note: Antonio Asprucci's lake garden of 1786, with the Ionic Tempietto di Esculapio on the islet and boats for hire on the water.

entries.name: Ingressi monumentali di Villa Borghese
entries.note: Six gateways from 1609 to 1827, by Flaminio Ponzio, Antonio Asprucci and Luigi Canina, on via Pinciana, piazzale San Paolo del Brasile, piazzale Flaminio, via Raimondi and via Aldrovandi.

entries.name: Porta Pinciana
entries.note: A gate of the Aurelian Walls at piazzale Brasile, enlarged by Honorius in 403 when the two semicircular flanking towers were added; earlier called Porta Turata and Porta Salaria Vetus.

entries.name: Ipogeo di via Livenza
entries.note: A frescoed and mosaicked underground hall of the later fourth century, found in 1923; currently closed for works, and admitting groups of no more than ten when it opens.

entries.name: Basilica di Sant'Eugenio
entries.note: Begun in 1942 by Enrico Pietro Galeazzi and Mario Redini as Pius XII's gift church for a quarter without a parish, and consecrated by him on 2 June 1951.

entries.name: Bioparco di Roma
entries.note: About 1,200 animals of about 150 species inside the park; the council resolved on a zoological garden in 1907, the company formed in 1909 and the garden opened in 1911.

entries.name: Casina di Raffaello
entries.note: Villa Borghese's playroom for ages three to fourteen, in Scipione Borghese's seventeenth-century lodge; closed Mondays and from 9 to 23 August.

entries.name: Explora - Il Museo dei Bambini di Roma
entries.note: The children's museum on via Flaminia, admitting Tuesday to Sunday in four timed sessions of an hour and three quarters, closed on Mondays.
